exposure: Transperineal sonography measurements (angle of progression, head-perineum distance)
outcome: Failed vacuum extraction (defined as need for cesarean delivery)
Adverse maternal outcomes (postpartum hemorrhage, obstetrical anal sphincter injuries)
Adverse neonatal outcomes (5-minute Apgar score <7, neonatal acidemia, admission to neonatal intensive care unit, neonatal trauma)
cohort: The study included 98 singleton pregnancies at term with sonographically confirmed fetal occiput posterior position before vacuum extraction, enrolled in 3 academic maternity units.
finding: Vacuum extraction was successful in 96% of cases, and a head-perineum distance of 38.5 mm or more, measured by transperineal ultrasound, was significantly associated with failed vacuum extraction.
mod_finding: Vacuum extraction was successful in 96% of cases with occiput posterior position, and a head-perineum distance of 38.5 mm or more was identified as a predictor of failed vacuum extraction, leading to a need for cesarean delivery.
